chapter: Last tours and the state of English jazz
title: Decline of traditional jazz in England and closing remarks, 1968-69
summary: Stagg laments pub jobs, club closures and bands working on the continent, notes the 1968 tours, and describes meeting people on the American trip.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: And this is really sad for England because to us we've gone down a stage. We got to a very good period where British traditional style bands were playing concerts. And big jobs, the Royal Festival Hall, the Conway Hall, which we've already mentioned. The Royal Festival Hall has symphony concerts and symphony orchestras. And the British traditional bands got to this stage where they were playing this type of job. And we now feel as if we've gone down a stage. That the English bands are now playing these pub jobs which are really few and far between. The Studio 51, the Ken Collier Club as it's known, was always open five nights a week. It was never opened on a Tuesday and a Thursday but it was open five nights a week. Doing two sessions on Sunday and an all-nighter from Saturday night to Sunday morning. They're no longer all-nighters. And just before we left to come to the States, the Studio 51 had a rhythm and blues band in there on Saturday night. And no traditional band there at all. Ken Collier plays there sometimes on a Saturday, sometimes on a Sunday. But it's pretty sad. The Barry Martin Band is about the only other traditional band to play there now. It's not open during the week at all. And this is the main, was the mecca of traditional jazz in London. The only other club running traditional style jazz is the 100 Club in Oxford Street. That is still open seven days a week but again is employing rhythm and blues bands and rock and soul bands and this type of music and private parties. Every now and again when the Kenny Ball or the Chris Barber Band or the Ackerbilt Band are back in England, they'll do one job at the 100 Club while they're in passing through. So it's come to this now. We've got plenty of London pubs having jazz bands in them, which are very nice for the public, but not too good for the musicians concerned. They're all virtually pick-up bands. There may be perhaps a dozen in the London area of these places going. So you can hear music for seven nights a week, which as I say is nice for the people but not too good for musicians. There are no small bands making a living out of traditional style jazz at the moment. The larger bands, people like Comfrey Littleton, only play when they're called for a job. It's not a regular band. They play society jobs a hell of a lot. And weddings or parties when they're called to play. The Kenny Ball, the Ackerbilt and the Chris Barber bands all play on the continent, mainly in Germany and Poland, majority of the year. The Ken Collier band has a steady amount of work around the country, but Ken Collier has his own devout followers, which he's always had, and can keep a steady amount of work going in this way. The jazz clubs are petering out as such. We had jazz clubs all over the country. We still have jazz clubs all over the country, but they're now farther apart and are more spasmodic, whereas they were once a week or once a fortnight. They're every other month now, this type of thing. Up to 1968, the last tour we had of a musician ourselves was Andrew Morgan, again only taking in one week in England, and again Italy and Belgium, this being of course that they're spending more time on the continent because the work is now on the continent. And sad but true, it isn't worth keeping an all-us musician. It cannot afford to keep an all-us musician in England when the Italian promoters are paying, and the Italian and Belgian promoters are paying most of the costs to bring them to Europe at all. The Olympia Brass Band came back again in September-October 1968, a larger unit this time, which was even better than the first, on their way to the Berlin Folk Festival. It stopped only two days, but managed a party and a recording. And from that to October 69, nothing has happened at all. It's been very, very quiet. The Baron Martin Band made an extensive tour of the United States, taking in the Orleans Jazz Festival. I myself have been keeping pretty quiet but active, dealing mainly with my own archives and files and recordings and letters and filing and keeping the music alive in England as much as possible. Up until now our visit here where we've been doing a lot of research and hearing a lot of music, meeting a lot of people, some great people we met, not just musicians, but just musicians. But other visitors in town, we've met a great lot of people, people like Eric Brown, who I only personally knew by letter. It was nice, and Yoshio, the Japanese trumpet player, it was nice to meet these guys who we only knew by letter and to meet in one place. And I've learnt a hell of a lot on this tour and I've got a tremendous amount of work to do now when I get back to add this to my own particular files to keep it going in England as much as possible. One good thing when we get back next week is that two days after we get back a manual sales arrives. So for a little while we'll have a bit of New Orleans back in England again for a short period. And that's just about the score. Another thing you say, Don? Nothing to write today. Nothing to write today.
